title: Laughing at yourself
hookLine: Nasruddin searches under the lamp; Montaigne sides with laughing Democritus over weeping Heraclitus
tomorrow: who was told "touch me not" on a morning of pure joy?

cards: Everybody has a moment they'd rather nobody had seen. A story told about Mulla Nasruddin, the wise fool of the folk tales: a neighbor finds him on his knees under a streetlamp. What did you lose?
My key. They both search. Nothing.
Where exactly did you drop it? In my house. Then why look out here?
Because, says Nasruddin, there's more light here.

teach.b: The joke is on Nasruddin, and then it's on us: we search where it's comfortable, not where we lost it. That's how these teaching tales work: you laugh at the fool, then recognize yourself.
That's one side of today's debate: laughing at yourself is wisdom. Montaigne, the French essayist, took that side.
In his essay on Democritus and Heraclitus, he sets two old philosophers side by side. Democritus laughed at human life; Heraclitus wept over it.
Montaigne prefers the laugher: we are, he says, less unhappy than vain, more foolish than wicked, and laughing at that takes us less seriously than weeping does. Now the other side, at its best.
Heraclitus's tears aren't silly. Some mistakes hurt people, and a laugh can be a way of dodging the repair. Tears take the damage seriously.
The weeper's best case: don't make a joke of what needs fixing. The laughers can answer: laughing at yourself isn't laughing off what you did to someone else.
It's refusing to make your own dignity the center of the universe. And one more look at the joke: Nasruddin never stops searching. He just admits where he's looking.

how: Nasruddin stories are told as teaching tales in which the listener laughs at the fool and then sees themselves. Montaigne's essay 'Of Democritus and Heraclitus' prefers the laughing philosopher to the weeping one.

o: seeing your own mistakes with a smile, not shame
never taking anything in life seriously at all
joking about others first so they can't joke about you

games.q: laugh or weep: tap the pairs.

s: Montaigne sided with the weeping philosopher
he preferred Democritus, the one who laughed.
in the story, Nasruddin lost his key inside his house
he searched outside because there was more light.
laughing at yourself means laughing off harm you did to others
laughing at your own fumbles isn't laughing off someone else's hurt.

games.q: a friend still jokes about the time he forgot his sister's wedding toast. she was really hurt. what's the weeper's best case here?
o: some mistakes hurt people; laughing first can skip the repair.
serious people never joke, so he should stop laughing at anything.
Montaigne taught that weeping is wiser than laughing.
games.why: Heraclitus's tears take the damage seriously. the laughers agree: laugh at your own dignity, not at someone else's hurt.

practice: Recall one recent moment you got wrong in a harmless, human way: a dropped plate, a wrong name, a door you pushed that said pull. Tell it to yourself like a Nasruddin story, out loud if you can, and let a smile come if it wants to.

wordCard.voice: Laughing at yourself: seeing your own fumbles with a smile, the Nasruddin and Montaigne way, without laughing off harm.

carryVoice: Your line: laugh. The fool under the streetlamp is all of us, now and then. Back tomorrow.

sources.ref: Montaigne, Essays I.50, 'Of Democritus and Heraclitus'
